value.overview: The Sooty Shearwater is a medium-large oceanic seabird of the southern Pacific and southern Atlantic regions. It spends most of its life at sea and comes ashore mainly to breed in large colonies on islands and coastal headlands. Famous for long-distance migrations, individuals may travel between subantarctic breeding grounds and productive waters of the North Pacific. In Costa Rica, it is a pelagic visitor, seen over Pacific waters rather than inland or along most sheltered beaches.
value.classification: The Sooty Shearwater belongs to the shearwater family Procellariidae, within the order Procellariiformes. Its scientific name is Ardenna grisea; it was formerly often placed in the genus Puffinus.
value.identification: This shearwater is about 40–45 cm long, with a long, narrow-winged shape and a dark brown to sooty overall appearance. The underparts are somewhat paler than the upperparts, and silvery or pale flashes may show across the underwings in good light. It has a relatively long, slender, all-dark bill. In flight, it uses rapid wingbeats followed by long glides close to the sea surface. It can resemble other dark shearwaters, especially Short-tailed Shearwater.
value.rangeHabitat: Sooty Shearwaters breed mainly on islands and coastal areas around New Zealand, southern Australia, and southern South America, nesting in burrows or beneath dense vegetation. Outside the breeding season they disperse widely across the Pacific, Atlantic, and sometimes Indian Ocean. They are strongly pelagic, favoring offshore waters, continental-shelf edges, fronts, and other areas rich in prey. In Costa Rica, the species occurs as an irregular to locally common or abundant non-breeding visitor in Pacific waters, especially offshore, with records concentrated from roughly May through October.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Birds leave southern-hemisphere breeding colonies after breeding and move northward through major oceanic routes. In Costa Rica, it is a non-breeding Pacific visitor, generally recorded offshore from May to October; it does not breed there.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in the southern hemisphere, generally during the austral spring and summer. Pairs nest colonially in burrows, crevices, or sheltered ground among vegetation, returning to colonies year after year. The female lays a single egg, and both adults share incubation and chick care. Chicks remain in the nest until well developed and are fed regurgitated food. Adults usually forage at sea, sometimes traveling considerable distances from colonies before returning to feed their young.
value.dietFeeding: The diet includes small fish, squid, crustaceans, and other marine animals. Sooty Shearwaters locate prey from the air and surface, then seize it while swimming or diving. They can make substantial underwater dives and may forage cooperatively in large flocks where prey is concentrated. Feeding areas often form around ocean fronts, upwellings, schools of fish, and other productive waters. They may also follow fishing vessels to take discarded fish or offal.
value.behavior: Sooty Shearwaters are highly social at sea and may gather in flocks numbering from dozens to many thousands. Their flight is typically a series of quick, deep wingbeats followed by stiff-winged glides close to the waves. They are powerful fliers capable of crossing entire ocean basins. At breeding colonies they are mainly nocturnal, which reduces exposure to some predators. On land they are much less agile than in flight and on water.

conservation.populationTrend: Suspected declining globally, although estimates and trend data vary among breeding colonies and regions. Some colonies have decreased while others have remained stable or increased, so the overall rate of decline is uncertain.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include accidental capture in fishing gear, reduced prey availability, changing marine conditions associated with climate change, disturbance or predation at breeding colonies, introduced predators on islands, and local harvesting of chicks. Offshore pollution and ingestion of marine debris may add further risks. In Costa Rica, the main relevant concerns are threats affecting pelagic waters, including fisheries bycatch, prey depletion, and marine pollution.
conservation.howToHelp: Support sustainable fisheries and efforts to reduce seabird bycatch, especially through safer fishing practices and effective monitoring. Protect breeding islands from introduced predators and disturbance, and support marine protected areas that safeguard important feeding zones. In Costa Rica, responsible boating, reduced plastic pollution, and reporting well-documented sightings through established bird-monitoring programs can improve knowledge of this uncommon offshore visitor.
